headline: Ask the Fix-It Expert: your electricity questions answered
standfirst: This week: dim fairy lights, big bills and a car that struggles to start
brief: Dan is great with a screwdriver, but his explanations worry us. Check his column before it reaches our readers.

body.t: “Why do my fairy lights get dimmer further along the string?” asks Joan from Leeds.
Joan, each lamp in a series string uses up some of the current, so there is less and less of it left for the lamps further along.

options: Current is used up only in the first lamp, not the others.
The current increases along the string, because the charges speed up as they pass through each lamp in turn.
Charge is conserved, so the current is the same throughout a series circuit; lamps transfer energy.
feedback: Current isn't used up anywhere in the circuit, in the first lamp or any other.
The current can't change around a series loop: charge doesn't pile up or disappear.
err.fix: Joan, the current is the same in every lamp in a series string, because charge is conserved; the lamps transfer electrical energy to light and thermal energy, so identical lamps should glow equally brightly, and a dimmer one is probably a different type from the rest.
keys: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit.
It is energy, not current or charge, that the lamps transfer.

body.t: When you switch them on, they light at once, even though the electrons in the wire drift along at only a fraction of a millimetre per second.
body.ok: It is correct: drift speeds are very small, but the electric field that sets all the electrons moving is established almost immediately around the whole circuit.

body.t: With 12 volts flowing through each lamp, even a small fault can show up.

options: Potential difference is measured across a component; it is current that flows through one.
Voltage flows through a wire but not through a lamp.
It should say 12 amps flowing, because volts and amps are the same thing.
feedback: Potential difference doesn't flow through anything. It exists between two points.
Potential difference (volts) and current (amps) are different quantities, so one can't replace the other.
err.fix: With a potential difference of 12 volts across each lamp, even a small fault can show up.
keys: Potential difference is across two points.
Current, not voltage, flows through a component.

body.t: “I fitted more lamps in my kitchen, all in parallel. What will that do to my bill?” asks Ravi from Hull.
Good news, Ravi: every extra lamp in parallel increases the total resistance of the circuit, so your supply will deliver less current and your bill will fall.

options: Parallel lamps do not change the total resistance at all.
Each extra parallel path reduces the total resistance, so the current and the power increase.
The total resistance increases, but the bill rises because the extra lamps are brighter and transfer more energy each second.
feedback: Each new branch gives the current another path, so the total resistance does change.
The direction is the problem here: adding a parallel branch makes the total resistance smaller, not larger.
err.fix: Sorry, Ravi: every extra lamp in parallel reduces the total resistance of the circuit, so your supply will deliver more current and your bill will rise.
keys: Adding a parallel branch reduces the total resistance.
The total current and power increase, so more energy is transferred.

body.t: Two identical 12-ohm lamps connected in parallel have a combined resistance of 6 ohms.
A filament lamp does not obey Ohm's law, because its resistance rises as the filament gets hotter.
body.ok: It is correct: the rising temperature increases the filament's resistance, so current is not proportional to potential difference.

body.t: “How much does my electric heater really cost?” asks Mei from Bristol.
Your heater is rated at 2 kW, Mei, which means that it uses up 2 kW of energy every hour.

options: A 2 kW heater uses 2 kW of energy every second instead, so in one hour it uses 7200 kW.
The kilowatt is a unit of current, not of energy.
The kilowatt is a unit of power: 2 kW means 2000 joules every second.
feedback: A kilowatt is already “per second” in its meaning, and it still isn't an amount of energy.
Current is measured in amperes. The watt is the unit of power.
err.fix: Your heater is rated at 2 kW, Mei, which means that it transfers 2000 joules of energy every second, or 2 kilowatt-hours every hour.
keys: Power is the rate of energy transfer.
Energy = power × time (2 kW for one hour is 2 kW h, which is 7.2 MJ).

body.t: “My headlights dim whenever I start the car. Is something wrong?” asks Tom from Cork.
Tom, a 12 V battery always delivers exactly 12 V at its terminals, however much current it supplies, so the dimming must be caused by a faulty headlamp.

options: A healthy battery delivers more than 12 V when the current is large.
A real battery has internal resistance, so a large current lowers its terminal potential difference.
The battery's emf falls to zero while the starter motor runs, and it returns to 12 V only once the engine has started.
feedback: When a battery delivers current, its terminal potential difference is below its emf, not above.
The emf doesn't vanish. Look for what reduces the potential difference available at the terminals.
err.fix: Tom, a battery has internal resistance, so the large current drawn by the starter motor lowers the potential difference at its terminals, and your headlamps dim for a moment; that is normal.
keys: A large current means a large $Ir$, so the terminal potential difference $\varepsilon - Ir$ falls.
